O V E R V I E W
What is the GNU Tool Chain?
A toolchain is the set of programs that turn human-readable source code into an executable. On Linux, that toolchain is GNU.
1
GCC
The GNU Compiler
Collection — front-ends
for C and C++.
2
Binutils
as (assembler), ld (linker),
ar (archiver) plus nm and
objdump.
3
glibc
The GNU C standard
library your programs link
against at build time.
4
GDB
The GNU debugger for
stepping through and
inspecting your programs.
gcc is a driver: one command that calls the preprocessor, compiler, assembler and linker in turn.
04
Why it matters: Naming the core programs — the compiler collection, the Binutils, the C library and the debugger — tells you which tool owns which job, so you know where to
look when a build fails.
C O M P I L E R D R I V E R S
gcc vs. g++
gcc g++
Front-end Compiles source as C Compiles source as C++
Std library You must add -lstdc++ / -lm Links libstdc++ automatically
.cpp files Needs the right flags/libs Handled natively
Best for C programs C++ programs
05
Why it matters: Picking the right driver decides whether the C++ standard library is linked for you, so choosing g++ for C++ code avoids the cryptic 'undefined reference' errors of
linking by hand.
C O M P I L A T I O N S T A G E S
From source to executable in four stages
One gcc hello.c command quietly runs four stages, each producing a new file.
1
Preprocess
tool: cpp
gcc -E
→ hello.i
Expands #include and
#define; strips comments.
2
Compile
tool: cc1
gcc -S
→ hello.s
Translates C into assembly
for the target CPU.
3
Assemble
tool: as
gcc -c
→ hello.o
Turns assembly into
machine-code object files.
4
Link
tool: ld
gcc
→ hello
Combines objects and
libraries into a binary.
06
Why it matters: A single gcc command quietly runs four stages, and seeing them shows where an error really comes from and which flag (-E, -S, -c) stops the build at each point
for inspection.
S T A G E S 1 & 2
Preprocessing & compilation
terminal
# 1 Preprocess: expand headers & macros
gcc -E hello.c -o hello.i
# 2 Compile: C source → assembly
gcc -S hello.i -o hello.s
# peek at the generated assembly
cat hello.s
Preprocessor (cpp)
Resolves #include, expands #define macros,
and removes comments — output is still C.
Compiler (cc1)
Parses the C, checks types, optimises, and
emits human-readable assembly (.s).
.i and .s files
Intermediate text files — handy for debugging
macros or inspecting generated code.
07
Why it matters: Producing the .i and .s intermediates lets you see headers and macros after expansion and read the generated assembly — how you debug tricky macros or
check what the compiler emits.
S T A G E 3
Assembly & object files
terminal
# 3 Assemble: .s → machine-code object
gcc -c hello.c -o hello.o
# inspect symbols and disassembly
nm hello.o
objdump -d hello.o
An object file holds compiled machine code, but it is not yet runnable — external
references still need to be linked.
Inside a .o file
•Machine code
Compiled instructions for each function.
•Symbol table
Names of functions & variables it defines or
needs.
•Relocation info
Placeholders the linker later fills with
addresses.
•No entry point
Cannot run on its own until linked.
08
Why it matters: An object file carries compiled machine code but no final addresses and cannot run on its own, which is exactly why a separate linking step is still required to
turn it into a program.
S T A G E 4
Linking: objects become a program
The linker (ld) stitches object files and libraries together, resolves every symbol to an address, and writes a single executable.
main.o
utils.o
libc / libs
ld ./app
OBJECTS + LIBRARIES LINKER EXECUTABLE
gcc main.o utils.o -o app — the driver invokes ld and links the C library for you.
09
Why it matters: The linker stitches object files and libraries together and resolves every symbol to a concrete address — the step that finally turns half-built pieces into one
runnable executable.
L I B R A R I E S
Static vs. shared libraries
Reusable code is packaged into libraries and linked into your program in one of two ways.
Static (.a)
Object code is copied into your binary at link time.
# archive objects
ar rcs libmath.a math.o
# link statically
gcc main.o -L. -lmath
Bigger binary • no runtime dependency
Shared (.so)
Loaded from disk at run time and shared across programs.
# build a shared object
gcc -shared -fPIC \
-o libmath.so math.c
gcc main.o -L. -lmath
Smaller binary • needs the .so at run time
10
Why it matters: Choosing between static and shared libraries trades a bigger, self-contained binary against a smaller one that depends on a .so at run time, so the right pick
depends on how you ship.
P U T T I N G I T T O G E T H E R
Building an executable, end to end
terminal
# 1 compile each source to an object
gcc -c main.c
gcc -c utils.c
# 2 link the objects into a binary
gcc main.o utils.o -o app
# 3 run it
./app
Result: 42
Step by step
1Compile
Each .c is turned into a .o object
independently.
2Link
gcc calls ld to merge the objects and
libraries.
3Executable
A single runnable binary (ELF) is produced.
4Run
./app loads and executes on the machine.
11
Why it matters: Compiling each source to an object and then linking them ties compile, link and run into one repeatable workflow you can reuse for any multi-file project rather
than one-off commands.
R E F E R E N C E
Essential gcc flags
A handful of options covers almost every everyday build.
-o <file> Name the output file -c Compile only — stop before linking
-Wall Enable common, useful warnings -g Add debug info for gdb
-O2 Optimise the generated code -I <dir> Add a header search path
-L <dir> Add a library search path -l<name> Link against a library
-std=c11 Select the language standard -E / -S Stop after preprocess / compile
12
Why it matters: A small set of everyday options — for naming output, compiling only, enabling warnings, adding debug info and optimising — covers almost every real build, so
they are worth knowing by heart.
S U M M A R Y
From source to executable, end to end
13
One gcc command drives the whole pipeline — from source, through preprocess, compile, assemble and link, to a running program.
Source
your C / C++
hello.c
Preprocess
cpp · gcc -E
→ hello.i
Compile
cc1 · gcc -S
→ hello.s
Assemble
as · gcc -c
→ hello.o
Link
ld · gcc
→ hello
Executable
runs on CPU
./hello
Libraries
libc + .a / .so linked in
W R A P - UP
Key takeaways
1gcc & g++ are drivers One command runs the preprocessor, compiler, assembler and linker.
2Compilation has four stages Preprocess → compile → assemble → link, each producing a new file.
3Object files are half-built They hold machine code and symbols but cannot run until linked.
4Linking makes the program ld resolves symbols and pulls in libraries to form one executable.
5Libraries: static or shared (.a) is baked into the binary; (.so) is loaded at run time.
14
Why it matters: Recapping the full path from source through preprocess, compile, assemble and link keeps the toolchain memorable as one connected process rather than a
handful of disconnected commands.
